reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Non-bullous impetigo, the most common form, begins as fragile vesicles or pustules that rupture to leave the characteristic golden-yellow (honey-coloured) crusts, often around the nose and mouth
Bullous impetigo produces larger flaccid blisters that leave a collarette of scale, and is driven by exfoliative toxins from Staphylococcus aureus
It is highly contagious and spreads readily among children through close contact and shared items
It frequently arises as a secondary infection over broken skin such as eczema, insect bites, or scabies, so look for and treat the underlying condition

Management centres on hygiene measures and antibacterial therapy: topical treatment for localised disease and systemic antibiotics for widespread, bullous, or systemically unwell cases, guided by local resistance patterns

Advise on reducing transmission, including handwashing, not sharing towels, and keeping children away from school or nursery until lesions have crusted or treatment has been under way for the recommended period
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a recognised complication following certain streptococcal strains, so watch for signs such as dark urine or oedema
Recurrent impetigo warrants consideration of staphylococcal carriage and decolonisation
reference.pathophysiology: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, alone or together. Organisms colonise and then invade skin whose barrier has been breached by minor trauma, bites, or pre-existing dermatoses. In bullous disease, staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis, causing intraepidermal separation and blister formation. The host inflammatory response and serous exudate dry to form the typical crusts. Certain nephritogenic streptococcal strains can trigger immune-complex-mediated post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex infection (grouped vesicles, may recur at the same site)
Eczema herpeticum in a child with atopic dermatitis
Acute allergic or irritant contact dermatitis with exudate and crusting
Bullous conditions such as bullous pemphigoid or linear IgA disease when blistering predominates
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in a systemically unwell young child
additionalInvestigations: Bacterial swab of exudate for culture and sensitivities in extensive, recurrent, or treatment-failing cases
Nasal and skin swabs to identify staphylococcal carriage in recurrent disease
Urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring if post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is suspected
Assessment for and treatment of underlying dermatoses such as eczema or scabies
redFlags: Rapidly spreading erythema, pain out of proportion, or systemic toxicity suggesting cellulitis or a deeper, necrotising infection
Widespread tender blistering and skin peeling in a young child indicating staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Features of eczema herpeticum such as punched-out erosions and systemic upset in an atopic patient
Dark urine, facial oedema, or hypertension after infection suggesting post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
reference.prognosis: Impetigo generally responds well to treatment and often heals without scarring, though it can recur, particularly with staphylococcal carriage or an untreated underlying skin condition; serious sequelae are uncommon but include post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
pitfalls: Missing an underlying dermatosis such as scabies or eczema that will drive recurrence if untreated
Failing to recognise eczema herpeticum and treating presumed impetigo with antibiotics alone
Overusing topical antibiotics and promoting resistance
Neglecting infection-control advice, allowing continued spread among household and school contacts
management: Topical antibacterial therapy such as fusidic acid or mupirocin, or topical hydrogen peroxide, for localised non-bullous disease

Oral antibiotics active against staphylococci and streptococci, such as flucloxacillin or a macrolide in penicillin allergy, for widespread, bullous or systemically unwell cases, guided by local resistance patterns
Hygiene measures including handwashing, not sharing towels and keeping lesions covered to reduce transmission
Identify and treat any underlying skin condition such as eczema, insect bites or scabies
Staphylococcal decolonisation with nasal and skin antiseptics in recurrent disease with confirmed carriage
Exclusion from school or nursery until lesions have crusted or antibiotic treatment has been under way for the recommended period
Monitor blood pressure and urinalysis where post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a concern
